extracted.intended_audience: academics applying for research grants (early to senior), particularly in Australia/UK but globally relevant
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, career-stage-aware advice and evaluative criteria for writing competitive academic research grant proposals (structure, voice, methodology, feasibility, resubmission). Emphasises conventions, time management, and funder-specific expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants are a learned writing genre with conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants are a learned writing genre with conventions; reading funded examples teaches the genre; structure carries meaning; reviewers expect conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To write well, study funded examples to learn conventions; ensure your proposal follows expected structural conventions so reviewers can quickly locate and interpret claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read funded examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading funded examples teaches the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successful applications as models for structure, phrasing, and level of evidence; mimic organizational conventions and rhetorical moves that worked for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confident, declarative voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice should be confident but not arrogant; 'We will determine X' not 'We hope to elucidate X'; avoid academic hedging that signals weakness; don't oversell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt declarative, authoritative phrasing to signal competence; remove hedging language; balance confidence with realistic claims so reviewers don't perceive hype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and signposting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use signposting throughout; topic sentences carry the argument; white space is your friend; headings and bold guide the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the argument easy to follow: clear headings, strong topic sentences, paragraph-level signposts, and abundant white space to help reviewers scan and understand key points quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time investment reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Major grant: 200+ hours; Smaller grant: 50-100 hours; build grant writing into normal weekly schedule; don't try to write a grant in 2 weeks before deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan realistic timelines and protect regular writing time across weeks/months; treat grant writing as a lengthy project rather than a last-minute sprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Write now, edit later" drafting approach
rubrics_metrics.description: First draft is exploration; don't edit while drafting; use Pomodoro-style writing sessions; get a complete draft 6+ weeks before deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate drafting from editing: aim for a full draft well before deadline, use focused timed sessions to produce text, and reserve extended revision time thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence of reviewers: 1) Self-edit (first 3-5 drafts), 2) Trusted peer in your field (next 2-3 drafts), 3) Senior mentor (1-2 reviews), 4) Outside-field reader (1 review for clarity), 5) Research office formatting check (final).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this ordered feedback pipeline to progressively move from developing argument to polishing language and compliance; each reviewer type has a distinct role (technical critique, strategic advice, clarity, formatting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the question and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with the question, not the methods; connect to public/societal/disciplinary concerns; don't assume reviewers share your enthusiasm; apply the 'So what?' test for every paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a clear, compelling research question and explicit statement of significance; continuously justify why the question matters to reviewers and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology must be specific and justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific enough to evaluate; cite published methods; justify your approach over alternatives; acknowledge limitations and pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide method detail sufficient for reviewers to assess rigor and feasibility, reference validated methodologies, explain why chosen methods are superior for your aims, and transparently describe limitations and mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic timeline with milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Realistic timeline with milestones is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a detailed, plausible schedule broken into milestones so reviewers can judge feasibility and progress expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility evidence (preliminary work, team, resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasibility evidence such as preliminary work, team composition, and available resources demonstrates the project's likelihood of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present concrete preliminary data, explain team roles and expertise, and document institutional support or infrastructure that enables the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator narrative appropriate for career stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigator narrative should match career stage: early-career highlight training and potential; mid-career differentiate from senior PIs; senior show leadership, consortia and strategic plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor CVs, track-record statements and future research vision to funder expectations and career stage; for person-focused schemes emphasise leadership and trajectory rather than only project specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with current debates in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement with the field's current debates is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate your question within contemporary disciplinary discussions, cite relevant literature, and explain how your project advances or challenges current thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limitations and pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state foreseeable weaknesses or risks and the mitigation strategies, which increases credibility and shows realistic planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish, formatting, and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish — no typos, formatting errors, length violations; research office formatting check as final step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure strict compliance with instructions, clean prose without errors, and final institutional checks for formatting and submission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience: treat rejection as normal
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection is the norm (funding rates 10-25%); successful PIs accumulate rejected grants; don't take it personally; read feedback once, set aside, return with senior colleague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage emotional response to rejection, maintain a file of past submissions, and review feedback strategically later with mentors for revision plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Address every critique substantively; use reviewer language verbatim where possible; acknowledge fair criticism; politely defend where critique is wrong; bold the changes in body text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a point-by-point response using reviewers' phrasing, document all changes, and clearly indicate revisions in the resubmission to make it easy for reviewers to see you've addressed concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARC Discovery Project formatting and criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: ARC Discovery Project: Project Description 6 pages (very short); Significance and Innovation 1 page; Research Plan 4 pages; evaluation criteria include Project Quality and Innovation, Investigator, Feasibility, Benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow strict page allocations and tailor each section to the specified criterion — be concise and prioritized given tight page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: NHMRC Investigator Grant expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: NHMRC Investigator Grant: grants the person, not the project (since 2019); track record and leadership central; emphasise future research vision over specific aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For person-focused schemes, foreground leadership, trajectory and capability to deliver a program of research rather than a narrow project plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mid-career researcher differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: ARC/NHMRC scores plateau in mid-career; need to differentiate from senior PIs; 'Field of Research' code matters for benchmarking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly articulate how your role and contributions differ from senior colleagues and choose appropriate field codes to ensure fair benchmarking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build collaborator network and mentor others
rubrics_metrics.description: Mid-career strategy includes building collaborator networks, serving as reviewer, and mentoring early-career colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate collaborative capacity and leadership through documented networks and mentoring activities as evidence of research maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small grants to build track record (early career)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early career: smaller grants build CV; learn the genre with low stakes; reuse content across applications; find mentor for mock review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target smaller funding to gain experience, reuse and adapt material sensibly, and solicit mock reviews from mentors to improve competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive writing habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Morning writing sessions; tiny goals (250 words/day); track progress; celebrate small wins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt sustainable daily writing habits, set modest measurable targets and monitor progress to make steady draft progress over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-life boundaries and sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant writing is work, but life continues; set boundaries around evening/weekend work; rest is part of productivity; emphasise long-term sustainability over heroic effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect personal time, plan sustainable workloads, and prioritise rest to avoid burnout while maintaining consistent progress on applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting/administrative final check
rubrics_metrics.description: Research office formatting check as final step in feedback hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before submission, have institutional research/administration staff verify compliance with formatting, budget, and submission rules to avoid administrative desk-rejections.
